explanations.explanation: This neuron flags conditional/hedging discourse connectives—most prominently the “in case you…” pattern—that introduce a precautionary or explanatory subordinate clause to set up background, warnings or clarifications.

This neuron is essentially an “ampersand detector” – it lights up on the “&” (and similarly rare non-alphanumeric connector glyphs) that tie together tickers, acronyms or compound names (e.g. “S & P”, “R & D”, etc.).

This neuron is simply a detector for the BPE sub‐token “g” – i.e. it lights up whenever the letter “g” ends up as its own token (as happens in e.g. abbreviations “e.g.,” in hyphenated names like “Hodgkinson,” or when “g” is split off at morphological boundaries).
This neuron is basically a little “C-V-C” detector for back-rounded vowels: it lights up on short word-pieces that follow a consonant–(u or o)–consonant pattern (un, ot, ug, uz, rot, und, etc.).

This neuron isn’t tracking any particular meaning—rather it’s a character‐level “trigram” detector, firing whenever it sees a common three-letter substring (e.g. “ram,” “rom,” “per,” “sch,” “phy,” “nom,” etc.) embedded in a word.
This neuron is a subword “ann” detector—it lights up on the letter sequence a-n-n, whether in names (e.g. “Kannada,” “Jagannath,” “Kanchipuram,” “Britannia”) or in words like “channel(ling).”
This feature is a detector for the “bl” consonant cluster in subword tokens—e.g. it spikes on “bl”-initial pieces in words like black, blind, blades (and related variants across languages).
This feature fires on mentions of the United States and its institutions—e.g. “U.S.,” “United States,” state names (Texas, North Carolina), American organizations or agencies.
This feature detects promotional calls-to-action—imperative “join us”/“join me” invitations urging the reader to participate in an event or activity.

This neuron is essentially an orthographic “D‐detector” – it lights up whenever a subword token contains the letter D/d (e.g. the “D” in Duke, December, Dodecane, Deckard/Denard, Down/Downward, Daltrey, the “d” in Perdana, pre-deceased, proceeding, off, etc.), regardless of the semantic context.

This neuron detects direct second‐person address in a hypothetical/instructional mood—i.e. “you” plus a modal (will, would, can, ’ll, etc.) used to give advice, instructions or promises to the reader.

This neuron fires whenever the text is talking about “stuff” (ingredients, chemicals, drugs, hormones, enzymes, etc.) and what you do to it (add, dissolve, regulate, fuel, mix, fold, avoid, etc.). In other words, it’s a detector for material-centric language – naming substances and the actions you take on them.

This feature is essentially an n-gram detector for the letter “P” paired with another letter (e.g. “BP,” “PB,” “AP,” “SP,” or “ap” in running text), so it spikes on both two-letter uppercase acronyms containing “P” and on the “ap” bigram inside longer words.

This neuron seems to fire on the kind of “call-to-action” and product-spec language you see in marketing or ads—imperative or event verbs (Send, Passed, Moved, Outsource) alongside specs and metrics (380 cst, 310 million, transmission, portals, etc.). It flags instructional/promotional tokens and the numerical or technical items that often follow them.

This feature is a grapheme/phoneme detector for the “sh” sequence (the /ʃ/ sound) in subword tokens—i.e. it spikes on any token containing that “sh” digraph (and related sequences like “shr,” “iss” in “scissor,” “Wissens­chaft,” etc.).
This neuron is a detector for the English “-st/-est” ending – it lights up on the subtoken carrying the superlative or ordinal suffix (e.g. “st” in 1st, “st” in worst, “hest” in highest).

The one thing all those high‐activation tokens share is that they’re subword pieces beginning with the letter “a” – e.g. the “a…” fragments in “Walking”/“alking,” “Hayden,” “Amber,” “Beaver,” “meander,” “swarming,” “Hiding,” “Mille lacs,” “Mashable,” etc. In other words, this neuron is detecting BPE subword chunks that start with “a.”

This feature fires on tokens that specify quantities or counts—cardinal and fractional numerals (four, eighteen, half-), and similar quantifier prefixes (mini-)—used in descriptions to enumerate items, sizes or measures.

This neuron lights up on “signposting” cues in explanatory or argumentative text—words and short phrases (e.g. answer, not, unlike, than, then, case, as, that, in) that introduce the key point, a contrast, comparison or structural pivot in exposition.

This neuron fires on the very first, often single‐letter or capitalized token that begins an entry or heading (e.g. the initial “B” in “Bionic,” “Brett,” “BAT,” “Bachman,” etc.), effectively marking the start of a title or named‐entity segment.
